paras: The lynching of Amos Jones took place at Hattiesburg, Mississippi, on the night of Saturday, August 8, 1903, when a mob broke into the jail, took Jones, a Black prisoner, from his cell, and hanged and shot him. Jones was accused of shooting the jailer, M. M. Sexton, during an attempt by prisoners to break jail. Wire reports of the jail break-in, carried from Massachusetts to Arizona, said the mob had tied up the sheriff and that the governor's order to protect Jones arrived too late.

According to a special dispatch to the Mobile Register from Hattiesburg, Jones and another Black prisoner named McElroy seized Sexton, intending to break jail. Two white youths, also prisoners, held the jailer while Jones shot him three times. McElroy escaped in the confusion and had not been caught. According to the Hattiesburg Daily Progress, Sheriff Batson and others then disarmed Jones and locked him in his cell.

Crowds formed around the jail, and prominent men urged them to desist; the wounded Sexton sent word to leave Jones unharmed. According to the wire account, the mob tied up Sheriff Batson, and the fire brigade refused to help disperse it. The Progress said instead that Batson "did everthing in his power to prevent violence."

The mob broke through a jail window and cut Jones out of his cell with chisels. Before a crowd the dispatch put at about 500 men and boys, he was dragged by a rope through town to Gordon Creek bridge, hanged to a telegraph pole and shot. The local paper said he was unconscious when dragged about half a mile, and that his body was "riddled with bullets" after the hanging.
The mob also threatened the white prisoners, but the sheriff sent them by train to Jackson. A militia order to protect Jones, sought by the sheriff, was not received until after the lynching.

The Progress reported a rumor that Black residents were organizing an attack and had been refused ammunition by merchants, adding that it "resulted in nothing." It also said Sexton's chances of recovery were "greatly augmented." No report of an inquest, of arrests among the mob, or of McElroy's recapture appears in the coverage.

The story first ran on August 9 as a Mobile Register special from Hattiesburg, printed by the Montgomery Advertiser under the headline "Chiseled Open Cell" and in shortened form by the Birmingham Age-Herald. The same dispatch ran in the Wichita Daily Eagle ("Mob Hangs for Killing"), the Indianapolis Journal and the Savannah Morning News. The New-York Tribune gave the event two lines under "A Lynching in Mississippi."

Headlines treated the shooting as fact: the Washington Times ran "Mob in Mississippi Lynches a Murderer" and the Bisbee Daily Review "Negro Convict Lynched." They repeated that Sexton's wounds were mortal, though the Progress reported him likely to recover. Weeklies in South Carolina, Washington state and Wisconsin carried condensed versions. The Oxford Eagle and Canton Times in Mississippi reprinted the full dispatch as news of "last week," and the Osceola Times in Arkansas ran it on August 22.

The Progress framed the episode around the officer, "one of our most respected citizens," and called the lynchers "the infuriated men." None of these white reports carried editorial comment on the lynching, and the coverage includes no account from the Black press.

The wire called Sexton the jailer with wounds "said to be fatal"; the Progress called him "Constable Sexton" and later reported his recovery likely. As the local paper writing two days later, the Progress is the closer source on his condition. The wire said Jones was thought dead before the hanging; the Progress, that he was unconscious when dragged. The Mobile Register dispatch counted three white prisoners sent to Jackson, while the Progress headline spoke of "Two White Boys."

reader.title: Lynching of Amos Jones
bases: A crowd broke into the Hattiesburg jail, took Jones from his cell, hanged him and shot his body (A2, A4, A9).

A mob the wire put at about 500 men and boys took Jones from jail over the sheriff's resistance and hanged and shot him, for the shooting of the jailer (A4, A9); no lawful authority was involved and the governor's order to protect him came too late (A4, A10).
The local Hattiesburg Daily Progress (A9) and the Mobile Register special and other wire dispatches (A2, A4) independently report the jail break-in, hanging and shooting of the body.

accounts.label: Mobile Register special / wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Jones and McElroy seized the jailer, Jones shot him; a crowd of about 500 tied the sheriff, cut Jones from his cell with chisels, dragged him to Gordon Creek bridge, hanged him to a telegraph pole and shot him, 'thought' dead before hanging; militia order too late.

accounts.label: Local paper (Hattiesburg Daily Progress)
accounts.gist: Sheriff Batson disarmed Jones and locked him up, then tried to prevent violence; the crowd stormed the jail, dragged the unconscious man half a mile, hanged him to a telephone pole and riddled the body; two white boys sent to Jackson; Sexton likely to recover.

framing.detail: The local Progress headlined 'Negro Shoots M. M. Sexton and Is Lynched by Mob', praised Sexton as a respected citizen and the sheriff's efforts, and reported a rumor of Black residents seeking ammunition, without editorial comment on the lynching.
Distant dailies ran the dispatch under headlines such as 'Mob Hangs for Killing', 'Chiseled Open Cell' and 'Negro Convict Lynched', describing the shooting as fact.
The Washington Times ('Mob in Mississippi Lynches a Murderer') and Worcester Spy ('Protect the Murderer') called Jones a murderer although Sexton had not died.

Wire wording; the local paper reported Sexton likely to recover, so 'mortally' is the wire's claim, not an outcome.

record_check.record: Sheriff Batson was tied up and the fire brigade refused to disperse the mob
record_check.dossier: Wire version; the local paper says only that Batson did everything in his power to prevent violence. Add that the mob also threatened the white prisoners, who were sent to Jackson.
The 1903-08-29 Opelousas Courier item is a medicine advertisement, not coverage; at least 17 white articles in 15 papers ran the story, Aug. 9-22.
